bottom_line: Prices are rising faster again. Inflation hit 3.8%, a 3-year high, and the Fed (the people who set interest rates) looks almost certain to raise rates in December, which makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone.

stories.title: Inflation is up, rate hike coming
stories.real: US inflation hit 3.8%, the highest in 3 years, and the Fed's own survey of businesses (the Beige Book) found price pressures spreading. Traders now put the chance of a December rate hike at 98%, and businesses say they plan more price hikes for 2027.
stories.you: Credit card, car loan and other borrowing costs are likely to stay high or climb, and everyday prices are still going up.

stories.title: New tariffs on 14 countries
stories.real: The White House rolled out a new round of tariffs (taxes on imported goods) aimed at 14 trading partners, including China and the EU, while offering lower rates to countries that sign trade deals. Economists say tariffs push prices up, which gives the Fed more reason to keep rates higher for longer.
stories.you: Imported stuff can get pricier, and loans may stay expensive longer.

stories.title: Stocks swung hard this week
stories.real: Fear about AI hit stocks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down almost 4% at one point. Then on Nov. 25 the Dow wiped out a 1,100-point loss in a late comeback, and AI stocks bounced back as buyers went looking for bargains.
stories.you: If you own index funds or tech stocks, your balance probably jumped around a lot this week. US markets are closed for Thanksgiving.

stories.title: Paychecks aren't keeping up
stories.real: The number of Amazon workers on food stamps has tripled, one example of workers getting a smaller slice of what the economy earns. The Fed's survey also says gas prices and interest rates are hurting car sales, and rising prices are squeezing holiday shoppers.
stories.you: If your raise hasn't kept up with your bills, you're not alone. That is the trend right now.

stories.title: Trump disputes official GDP numbers
stories.real: President Trump called the government's GDP figures (the main measure of how much the economy is growing) 'fake' and demanded an investigation of the Commerce Department, which publishes them.
stories.you: Official economic numbers are what the Fed and investors use to make decisions, so a fight over whether they can be trusted matters to markets.
